meta.title: Arabic Alphabet
meta.subtitle: 31 letters, 16 signs and 7 rules · 101 cards
meta.desc: How Arabic is written and read, before the first word: the first deck of the Arabic collection. 54 notes — the 28 letters with hamza (ء), tāʔ marbūṭa (ة) and alif maqṣūra (ى); 16 signs, which are what a vowelled word carries beyond its letters (the three short vowels, the sukūn, the shadda, the three tanwīn endings, the long vowels and the two diphthongs, the madda, the dagger alif and the lām-alif); and 7 rules (the direction of the script, the six letters that join on one side only, the hamza's carriers, the article before a moon letter and before a sun letter, the hamzat al-waṣl, and why a text printed without vowels can be read more than one way). A letter or a sign is two cards, each with its own schedule: see it and recall its name and sound, or see the name and sound and recall it. A rule is one card: a question over a spelling. THE ORDER: the direction of the script, then the three short vowels and the sukūn, because every example word from there on is printed with them; then the letters in their standard order; then everything else, the rules of the article last. WHY THE SIGNS ARE HERE: every headword of the level decks is printed with its vowels, and of Arabic A1's first 500 words 453 carry a fatḥa, 199 a sukūn, 183 a kasra, 74 a ḍamma, 64 a shadda and 20 a tanwīn, 126 spell a long ā and 74 write a hamza on a carrier. THE PACE, since a deck cannot set it: at the default of ten new cards a day this deck takes 11 days. WHERE IT COMES FROM: nothing on a card was written for this deck. Each sound is the IPA value and the ‘English approximation’ of Wikipedia, ‘Help:IPA/Arabic’, revision 1380899154 — where that page says a sound has no equivalent in English (ع, ط), the card says so in its words; a letter's four shapes, the rules of joining, the hamza, the vowel signs, nunation, gemination, the sukūn and the dagger alif are sentences and table cells of Wikipedia, ‘Arabic alphabet’, revision 1386233872; the rule of the article and its two lists of letters are Wikipedia, ‘Sun and moon letters’, revision 1378024909. A quoted sentence keeps Wikipedia's own romanisation (fatḥah, ʾalif); a name's own romanisation is in the scheme the level decks use (ʔ for hamza, ʕ for ʿayn), and the Arabic names are vowelled as the English Wiktionary vowels them (kaikki.org). Every example word is a card of Arabic A1, the first that shows the letter or sign in the order A1 is dealt, with A1's romanisation and meaning and a speaker beside it. Text: CC BY-SA 4.0.

fields.Ask: Which way is Arabic written, and how many letters has it?
fields.Says:
written from right-to-left in a cursive style, and includes 28 letters
The Arabic alphabet is always cursive and letters vary in shape depending on their position within a word.

fields.Named: فَتْحَة fatḥa — a
fields.Sound: /a/ cat in British English, only approx. in American English
fields.Notes: Short vowels may be written with diacritics placed above or below the consonant that precedes them in the syllable, called ḥarakāt.
fields.Example:
ذَهَبَḏahabato go
عَرَفَʕarafato know

fields.Named: كَسْرَة kasra — i
fields.Notes: Approximated to English "I" (as in "pick")
fields.Example:
آسِفʔāsifsorry
شَرِبَšaribato drink

fields.Named: ضَمَّة ḍamma — u
fields.Notes: Approximated to English "U" (as in "put")
fields.Example:
كُلّkullevery; all
رَجُلrajulman

fields.Named: سُكُون sukūn — no vowel with this consonant letter
fields.Value: sukūn — no vowel with this consonant letter
fields.Sound: no vowel with this consonant letter
fields.Notes: we would instead indicate that the l is followed by no vowel by marking it with a diacritic called sukūn
fields.Example:
لَيْسَlaysais not
شَيْءšayʔthing; something

fields.Shapes: اaloneاstartـاmiddleـاend
fields.Named: أَلِف ʔalif — ā
fields.Notes:
a long ā following a consonant other than a hamza is written with a short a sign (fatḥah) on the consonant plus an ʾalif after it
six letters (و ,ز ,ر ,ذ ,د ,ا) can only be linked to their preceding letter
fields.Example:
كَانَkānato be (in the past); was
أَرَادَʔarādato want

fields.Shows: ا د ذ ر ز و
fields.Ask: What do these six letters never do?
fields.Says: Generally, letters in the same word are linked together on both sides by short horizontal lines, but six letters (و ,ز ,ر ,ذ ,د ,ا) can only be linked to their preceding letter.
fields.Example:
قَالَqālato say
جَاءَjāʔato come

fields.Shapes: بaloneبـstartـبـmiddleـبend
fields.Named: بَاء bāʔ — b
fields.Example:
بَعْضbaʕḍsome
بَقِيَbaqiyato stay, to remain

fields.Shapes: تaloneتـstartـتـmiddleـتend
fields.Named: تَاء tāʔ — t
fields.Example:
تَعَلَّمَtaʕallamato learn
تَذَكَّرَtaḏakkarato remember

fields.Shapes: ثaloneثـstartـثـmiddleـثend
fields.Named: ثَاء ṯāʔ — ṯ
fields.Example:
ثَانٍṯāninsecond
ثَالِثṯāliṯthird

fields.Shapes: جaloneجـstartـجـmiddleـجend
fields.Named: جِيم jīm — j
fields.Notes: The letter ج represents [ɡ] in Egypt and [ʒ] in the Levant and the Maghreb
fields.Example:
جَيِّدjayyidgood
جَدِيدjadīdnew

fields.Shapes: حaloneحـstartـحـmiddleـحend
fields.Named: حَاء ḥāʔ — ḥ
fields.Sound: /ħ/ hello, but pronounced in the back of the throat (pharyngeal)
fields.Example:
حَاوَلَḥāwalato try
حَيَاةḥayāhlife

fields.Shapes: خaloneخـstartـخـmiddleـخend
fields.Named: خَاء ḵāʔ — ḵ
fields.Example:
خَرَجَḵarajato go out, to leave
خَيْرḵayrgood, goodness

fields.Shapes: دaloneدstartـدmiddleـدend
fields.Named: دَال dāl — d
fields.Notes: six letters (و ,ز ,ر ,ذ ,د ,ا) can only be linked to their preceding letter
fields.Example:
دَخَلَdaḵalato enter, to go in
دَقِيقَةdaqīqaminute

fields.Shapes: ذaloneذstartـذmiddleـذend
fields.Named: ذَال ḏāl — ḏ
fields.Notes: six letters (و ,ز ,ر ,ذ ,د ,ا) can only be linked to their preceding letter
fields.Example: ذَهَبَḏahabato go

fields.Shapes: رaloneرstartـرmiddleـرend
fields.Named: رَاء rāʔ — r
fields.Sound: /r/ "tapped" or "trilled" r; Spanish perro
fields.Notes: six letters (و ,ز ,ر ,ذ ,د ,ا) can only be linked to their preceding letter
fields.Example:
رَأَىraʔāto see
رِجْلrijlleg; foot

fields.Shapes: زaloneزstartـزmiddleـزend
fields.Named: زَاي zāy — z
fields.Notes: six letters (و ,ز ,ر ,ذ ,د ,ا) can only be linked to their preceding letter
fields.Example:
زَوْجَةzawjawife
زَوْجzawjhusband

fields.Shapes: سaloneسـstartـسـmiddleـسend
fields.Named: سِين sīn — s
fields.Example:
سَمِعَsamiʕato hear
سَبَبsababreason

fields.Shapes: شaloneشـstartـشـmiddleـشend
fields.Named: شِين šīn — š
fields.Example:
شَخْصšaḵṣperson
شَعَرَšaʕarato feel

fields.Shapes: صaloneصـstartـصـmiddleـصend
fields.Named: صَاد ṣād — ṣ
fields.Sound: /sˤ/ close to saw, emphatic and pharyngealized /s/
fields.Example:
صَحِيحṣaḥīḥcorrect, right
صَغِيرṣaḡīrsmall; young

fields.Shapes: ضaloneضـstartـضـmiddleـضend
fields.Named: ضَاد ḍād — ḍ
fields.Sound: /dˤ/ emphatic and pharyngealized /d/, no equivalent, can be approximated to RP dawn
fields.Example:
ضَوْءḍawʔlight
ضَحِكَḍaḥikato laugh

fields.Shapes: طaloneطـstartـطـmiddleـطend
fields.Named: طَاء ṭāʔ — ṭ
fields.Sound: /tˤ/ emphatic and pharyngealized /t/, no equivalent
fields.Example:
طِفْلṭiflchild
طَوِيلṭawīllong; tall

fields.Shapes: ظaloneظـstartـظـmiddleـظend
fields.Named: ظَاء ẓāʔ — ẓ
fields.Notes: The letter ظ represents either [ðˤ] or [zˤ], depending on the speaker's dialect
fields.Example:
ظَهْرẓahrback
ظُهْرẓuhrnoon

fields.Shapes: عaloneعـstartـعـmiddleـعend
fields.Named: عَيْن ʕayn — ʕ
fields.Sound: /ʕ/ no equivalent in English (voiced pharyngeal fricative or voiced creaky-voiced pharyngeal approximant)
fields.Example:
عَلَّمَʕallamato teach
عَمِلَʕamilato work; to do

fields.Shapes: غaloneغـstartـغـmiddleـغend
fields.Named: غَيْن ḡayn — ḡ
fields.Sound: /ɣ/ like gallon, but with a guttural sound further back in the mouth (uvular). Alternatively like French paris
fields.Example:
غَيْرḡayrother than; not
غُرْفَةḡurfaroom

fields.Shapes: فaloneفـstartـفـmiddleـفend
fields.Named: فَاء fāʔ — f
fields.Example:
فَعَلَfaʕalato do
فَهِمَfahimato understand

fields.Shapes: قaloneقـstartـقـmiddleـقend
fields.Named: قَاف qāf — q
fields.Sound: /q/ like skit, but further back in the mouth (uvular)
fields.Example:
قَرَأَqaraʔato read
قَامَqāmato stand up; to carry out

fields.Shapes: كaloneكـstartـكـmiddleـكend
fields.Named: كَاف kāf — k
fields.Example:
كَتَبَkatabato write
كَثِيرkaṯīrmany, much

fields.Shapes: لaloneلـstartـلـmiddleـلend
fields.Named: لَام lām — l
fields.Notes:
[ɫ] (tool)
[ɫ] occurs only in the word Allah
fields.Example:
لَذِيذlaḏīḏdelicious
لَيْلَةlaylanight (one night)

fields.Shapes: مaloneمـstartـمـmiddleـمend
fields.Named: مِيم mīm — m
fields.Example:
مَكَانmakānplace
مَرَّةmarratime (once, twice …)

fields.Shapes: نaloneنـstartـنـmiddleـنend
fields.Named: نُون nūn — n
fields.Example:
نَظَرَnaẓarato look
نَسِيَnasiyato forget

fields.Shapes: هaloneهـstartـهـmiddleـهend
fields.Named: هَاء hāʔ — h
fields.Example:
هَاتِفhātiftelephone
هَدِيَّةhadiyyapresent, gift

fields.Shapes: وaloneوstartـوmiddleـوend
fields.Named: وَاو wāw — w
fields.Notes:
/uː/ cool
long ū as a sign for short u (ḍammah) plus a wāw
six letters (و ,ز ,ر ,ذ ,د ,ا) can only be linked to their preceding letter
fields.Example:
وَقْتwaqttime
وَجَدَwajadato find

fields.Shapes: يaloneيـstartـيـmiddleـيend
fields.Named: يَاء yāʔ — y
fields.Notes:
/iː/ machine
long ī is written as a sign for short i (kasrah) plus a yāʾ
fields.Example:
يَوْمyawmday
يَدyadhand

fields.Named: ā
fields.Notes: a long ā following a consonant other than a hamza is written with a short a sign (fatḥah) on the consonant plus an ʾalif after it
fields.Example:
أَجَابَʔajābato answer
اِسْتَطَاعَistaṭāʕato be able to, can

fields.Named: ū
fields.Notes: long ū as a sign for short u (ḍammah) plus a wāw
fields.Example:
أُسْبُوعʔusbūʕweek
صُورَةṣūrapicture, photo

fields.Named: ī
fields.Notes: long ī is written as a sign for short i (kasrah) plus a yāʾ
fields.Example:
كَبِيرkabīrbig; old (of a person)
طَرِيقṭarīqroad, way

fields.Named: ay
fields.Notes: y with sukūn will be unambiguously read as the diphthong /aj/, and w with sukūn will be read /aw/
fields.Example:
بَيْتbaythouse, home
عَيْنʕayneye

fields.Named: aw
fields.Notes: y with sukūn will be unambiguously read as the diphthong /aj/, and w with sukūn will be read /aw/
fields.Example:
نَوْعnawʕkind, sort
صَوْتṣawtvoice; sound

fields.Named: شَدَّة šadda — consonant doubled/geminated
fields.Notes: Gemination is the doubling of a consonant. Instead of writing the letter twice, Arabic places a W-shaped sign called shaddah above it.
fields.Example:
أُمّʔummmother
أَحَبَّʔaḥabbato love, to like

fields.Named: هَمْزَة hamza — ʔ
fields.Notes: The hamza /ʔ/ (glottal stop) can be written either alone, as if it were a letter, or with a carrier, when it becomes a diacritic.
fields.Example:
مَاءmāʔwater
جُزْءjuzʔpart

fields.Ask: What do these four have in common?
fields.Says: The hamza /ʔ/ (glottal stop) can be written either alone, as if it were a letter, or with a carrier, when it becomes a diacritic.
fields.Example:
أَهْلًاʔahlanhi, welcome
إِلَىʔilāto
هٰؤُلَاءِhāʔulāʔithese
دَائِمًاdāʔimanalways

fields.Named: مَدَّة madda — ʔā
fields.Notes: Hamzat al-madd (آ) indicates a long /ʔ/ + /aː/ sound as in آسف ʾāsif /ʔaː.sif/ "sorry"
fields.Example:
آخِرʔāḵirlast
آسِفʔāsifsorry

fields.Shapes: ةaloneـةend
fields.Named: تَاء مَرْبُوطَة tāʔ marbūṭa — -a / -at
fields.Notes:
Used in final position only as a marker of feminine gender for nouns and adjectives.
in Modern Standard Arabic it is only pronounced as such if the word is suffixed with a case ending or it is in the construct state, otherwise it is unpronounced or pronounced as /h/
fields.Example:
سَنَةsanayear
سَيَّارَةsayyāracar

fields.Shapes: ىaloneـىend
fields.Named: أَلِف مَقْصُورَة ʔalif maqṣūra — ā
fields.Notes: Used only at the end of some words as a spelling convention for etymological reasons.
fields.Example:
مَتَىmatāwhen?
عَلَىʕalāon

fields.Named: تَنْوِين tanwīn — -an
fields.Notes:
In written Arabic, nunation is indicated by doubling the vowel diacritic at the end of the word, e.g. شُكْرًا šukran [ʃukran] 'thank you'.
is the addition of a final -n to a noun or adjective. The vowel before it indicates grammatical case.
fields.Example:
مَرْحَبًاmarḥabanhello
شُكْرًاšukranthank you

fields.Named: تَنْوِين tanwīn — -in
fields.Notes: is the addition of a final -n to a noun or adjective. The vowel before it indicates grammatical case.
fields.Example:
غَالٍḡālinexpensive
ثَانٍṯāninsecond

fields.Named: تَنْوِين tanwīn — -un
fields.Notes: is the addition of a final -n to a noun or adjective. The vowel before it indicates grammatical case.

fields.Named: lā
fields.Notes:
some letter combinations are written as ligatures (special shapes), notably lām-alif لا
which is the only mandatory ligature
fields.Example:
لَاlāno; not
ثَلَاثَةṯalāṯathree

fields.Named: أَلِف خَنْجَرِيَّة ʔalif ḵanjariyya — ā
fields.Notes: It indicates a long /aː/ sound for which alif is normally not written.
fields.Example:
هٰذَاhāḏāthis (masculine)
هٰذِهِhāḏihīthis (feminine)

fields.Ask: How is the article read before a moon letter?
fields.Says:
When the Arabic definite article (الْـ) is followed by a moon letter, no assimilation takes place.
ا ب ج ح خ ع غ ف ق ك م ه و ي
fields.Example:
الْآنَal-ʔānanow
الْأَحَدal-ʔaḥadSunday

fields.Ask: How is the article read before a sun letter?
fields.Says:
When followed by a sun letter, the /l/ of the Arabic definite article al- assimilates to the initial consonant of the following noun, resulting in a doubled consonant.
al-shams ('the Sun') becomes ash-shams (assimilating the lām), while al-qamar ('the Moon') remains unchanged
ت ث د ذ ر ز س ش ص ض ط ظ ل ن
fields.Example:
السَّبْتas-sabtSaturday
اللَّٰهallāhGod

fields.Ask: What does this sign over an alif say, and where is it written?
fields.Says: It indicates that the ʾalif is not pronounced as a glottal stop (written as the hamza), but that the word is connected to the previous word (like liaison in French). Outside of vocalised liturgical texts, the waṣla is usually not written.
fields.Example:
اِمْرَأَةimraʔawoman
اِبْنibnson

fields.Ask: Why can this be read in more than one way?
fields.Says:
Users of Arabic usually write long vowels but omit short ones, so readers must utilize their knowledge of the language in order to supply the missing vowels.
the word qalb, "heart", is written qlb, and the word qalaba "he turned around", is also written qlb
In the Arabic handwriting of everyday use, in general publications, and on street signs, short vowels are typically not written.
